lesson_title: The Earth Is an Avocado: Inside Our Planet
hook_text: Nobody has ever been down there. So how do we know the earth's core is liquid?
clip_script: Cut an avocado in half and you are holding a model of the earth. The skin is the crust — look how thin it is, and that is exactly right: five to seventy kilometres, on a planet six thousand three hundred kilometres to the middle. Every mine, every borehole, every mountain, all of it happens in the skin. The green flesh is the mantle: two thousand nine hundred kilometres of it, eighty-four per cent of the whole earth. And here is what people get wrong — it is NOT a lake of lava. It is solid rock. Just, near the top, soft enough to ooze, like butter that has sat in a Durban kitchen all afternoon. Still butter, still solid, but it sags. That soft band is what lets the continents move. The pip is the core, and it has two parts: liquid iron sloshing on the outside, which is the only reason your compass works, and a solid iron ball at the very centre, five to six thousand degrees, as hot as the surface of the sun. Why does the hottest place not melt? Because it is squeezed so hard the iron simply cannot spread out. Pressure beats heat.
visual_style: A halved avocado dissolving into a cutaway earth, each part labelling itself; a slow-motion sag of warm butter; a compass needle swinging as liquid metal churns.
mood: Kitchen-table wonder — the ordinary object hiding the whole planet.
pacing: Unhurried through the three parts, quickening on the two myths, landing on 'pressure beats heat'.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find out how the silence of a seismic wave proved the core is liquid.
